content.text: Belt drives are on almost every machine around you — the alternator belt in a car engine, the conveyor belt in a factory, the drive belt in a washing machine. Every time you calculate belt width b, you're essentially asking: "How wide does this belt need to be to carry this much power without snapping?" That's exactly what you just solved.

Common mistake — Using μ_s×θ_s vs μ_L×θ_L — you must pick the combination that gives the smaller value of e^(μθ), because that's the condition where slip happens first. Students often just use μ_s×θ_s without checking both. Always compute both and use the smaller one.

items: • Full belt drive problem: find angle of contact, belt velocity, centrifugal tension, tight/slack side tensions, and belt width. Common exam Q
• Apply T₁/T₂ = e^(μθ) correctly using the smaller pulley's angle.
• Find belt width b from the mass-per-unit-length expression and power equation.
